lesson.title: Locating answers quickly
lesson.text: In an easy Multiple Choice set, most questions point you to one paragraph. Use names, numbers and distinctive terms in the question (for example Germany, 70°C, membrane) as signposts, then read the whole sentence around them. The answer usually paraphrases one sentence. Avoid choosing an option simply because it shares a word with the passage.
lesson.example: Passage: "Few visitors came in winter because the road was often closed." Question: Why were there few winter visitors? Correct idea: access was difficult. A tempting wrong option would be the weather was too cold, because it sounds logical but is not stated.

questions.q: For much of the twentieth century, city roofs were generally seen as
questions.evidence: the flat roofs of city buildings were regarded as wasted space
questions.explanation: "Wasted space" is paraphrased as "an area of little value". D describes the present day, not the twentieth century. Maintenance workers are mentioned, but the passage never says roofs were dangerous (C).

questions.q: According to paragraph A, intensive green roofs differ from extensive ones because they
questions.evidence: Intensive roofs ... have much deeper soil, can support shrubs and even small trees
questions.explanation: "Shrubs and small trees" = "bigger plants". A describes extensive roofs. Growing food (B) and new buildings (D) are not what distinguishes the two types.

questions.q: What was the main contribution of German research in the 1960s and 1970s?
questions.evidence: tested new waterproof membranes ... developed lightweight growing materials ... turned what had been a risky experiment into a practical building method
questions.explanation: The research made green roofs practical. A is contradicted: "The idea ... is very old". C is a word-match trap, because the grants came later from cities, not from the research.

questions.q: What does the writer say about the temperature of a planted roof on a hot day?
questions.evidence: A planted roof ... tends to stay close to the temperature of the surrounding air
questions.explanation: "Stay close to" = "remains similar to". The figure of 70°C refers to a conventional roof (B). A goes further than the passage.

questions.q: What point does the writer make about green roofs and rainwater?
questions.evidence: planted roofs "could hold between half and nine-tenths of the rain from a light shower. In heavy, prolonged storms ... the benefit is considerably smaller"
questions.explanation: The benefit changes with the intensity of the rain. A and D use extreme wording the passage does not support. Storing rain for use in buildings (C) is not mentioned.

questions.q: Why may a green roof last longer than a conventional roof?
questions.evidence: the extra layers protect the waterproof membrane from sunlight and sudden changes in temperature, which are the main causes of its decay
questions.explanation: "Sunlight and temperature changes" = "damaging conditions". Reinforcement (B) is mentioned only as a cost for older buildings.

questions.q: What is the writer's main purpose in paragraph G?
questions.evidence: The most common reason for failure is poor planting ... Green roofs work best ... when they are treated ... as small ecosystems suited to their surroundings
questions.explanation: The paragraph's central message concerns suitable planting. City policies are mentioned only briefly (B), and the writer never argues that every building needs a green roof (A).

title: When Every Town Kept Its Own Time

lesson.title: Watch for "more seriously", "however" and "rather than"
lesson.text: Signal words show which idea the writer considers most important or which idea is being corrected. If a passage says "X caused confusion; more seriously, it caused Y", a question about the most serious problem wants Y, not X. Likewise, "A rather than B" means A is true and B is not. Distractors are often built from the idea that the signal word pushes aside.
lesson.example: Passage: "The festival was moved to spring, partly because of cost but mainly because of the risk of storms." Question: What was the main reason for the change? Answer: the weather risk. Cost is the distractor, because it was only a partial reason.

questions.q: Before the railway era, towns decided the time by
questions.evidence: Each town set its clocks by the sun, declaring noon to be the moment when the sun stood highest
questions.explanation: "Set its clocks by the sun" = "observing the position of the sun". The observatory (A) only becomes relevant later, in Paragraph C.

questions.q: Why were differences in local time unimportant for many centuries?
questions.evidence: a journey between towns took many hours, and a difference of a few minutes went unnoticed
questions.explanation: Slow travel meant small differences did not matter. D is the opposite of the passage, which says towns kept different times. B is never mentioned.

questions.q: According to paragraph B, what was the most serious consequence of using different local times on the railways?
questions.evidence: More seriously ... drivers working to different times could find themselves on the same section of line ... with a real risk of collision
questions.explanation: The signal "More seriously" marks the most serious consequence. A, B and C are real problems but are presented as less serious.

questions.q: What does the writer find surprising about the situation in Britain?
questions.evidence: by the mid-1850s the great majority of public clocks ... showed Greenwich time. Remarkably, the law did not catch up until 1880
questions.explanation: "Remarkably" shows what the writer finds surprising: the practice came before the law. B and D contradict the passage. C wrongly attaches the law to the year 1840.

questions.q: What does the writer say about the time zones introduced in North America in 1883?
questions.evidence: organised by the railways rather than by the government, and it was not universally welcomed ... a number of cities refused
questions.explanation: Both parts of C are supported. A is contradicted by "rather than by the government", and B by "cities refused".

questions.q: What was the result of the 1884 conference in Washington?
questions.evidence: choose a single line of longitude ... from which distances and times ... could be measured. They selected the meridian passing through Greenwich
questions.explanation: A "prime meridian" is paraphrased as "a reference line". A is contradicted by "did not create a worldwide system of time zones". C is contradicted by the half-hour offsets.

questions.q: What is the main point of paragraph F?
questions.evidence: It changed the way people related to time ... factories, offices and schools began their work at fixed hours
questions.explanation: This is the paragraph's central idea. C is contradicted: "not by scientists or governments". Phones (A) appear only as a modern example, and the paragraph never says zones are unnecessary.

lesson.title: Questions about theories and evidence
lesson.text:
Science passages often present a theory, the evidence for it, and then evidence against it. Keep three things separate: what a theory claims, what a study found, and what the writer concludes.

A distractor may state a theory's claim as if it had been proved, or state the writer's conclusion more strongly than the writer does. Watch hedging words such as may, suggests, appears and some.
lesson.example: Passage: "The results suggest that sleep may help memory, but the sample was small." Question: What does the writer say about the results? A good answer: they are promising but limited. A trap: they prove that sleep improves memory, because it turns "suggest" into "prove".

questions.q: What is the main purpose of paragraph A?
questions.evidence: explaining why it happens has become an intriguing puzzle for psychologists
questions.explanation: The paragraph builds towards this question, which the rest of the passage then explores. C is only a supporting detail. A and D are not discussed.

questions.q: According to paragraph B, contagious yawning
questions.evidence: has been reliably recorded in humans and in chimpanzees
questions.explanation: "Reliably recorded" = "clearly shown". A and D are contradicted by the passage. The evidence for dogs is described as "less consistent", which does not support C.

questions.q: What did experiments with young children show?
questions.evidence: Children under the age of about four rarely yawned in response
questions.explanation: "Rarely" = "seldom". D reverses the pattern described. Family members (C) are mentioned in Paragraph D, not in these experiments.

questions.q: Why do supporters of the empathy theory refer to yawns caught from family members?
questions.evidence: people were more likely to 'catch' a yawn from a family member ... If contagious yawning were a simple automatic reflex ... the relationship between the two people should make no difference
questions.explanation: The example is used to show that the relationship matters. A is the view it argues against. C is too extreme, because strangers are "least likely", not "never".

questions.q: According to the temperature theory, people should
questions.evidence: people should yawn less when the air around them is very hot
questions.explanation: This is stated directly as the theory's prediction. A is the opposite. D contradicts the claimed cooling effect.

questions.q: What have recent large studies suggested?
questions.evidence: found only a weak connection between how often people catch yawns and how they score on tests of empathy
questions.explanation: "Only a weak connection" supports "weaker than believed". B reverses the age finding. D is contradicted by the mention of tiredness.

questions.q: Which statement best reflects the writer's conclusion?
questions.evidence: contagious yawning is influenced by a mixture of biological and social factors
questions.explanation: "A mixture of factors" = "more than one cause". The writer hedges ("It is possible"), so the strong claims in A and D are unsupported. B contradicts "surprisingly deep questions".

lesson.title: Numbers and comparisons
lesson.text: When a question contains a number, a percentage or a comparison word (more, less, cheaper, faster), check exactly what is being compared with what. Distractors often use the correct figure but attach it to the wrong thing, or they reverse a comparison. Read the whole sentence containing the number, not just the number.
lesson.example: Passage: "The new engine uses 30% less fuel than the older model, although it costs more to build." Question: What advantage does the new engine have? Answer: lower fuel use. A likely trap: it is 30% cheaper, which uses the right number for the wrong thing.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the last sentence of paragraph A?
questions.evidence: Supporters describe these buildings as the future ... critics see them as an expensive solution
questions.explanation: The sentence sets two opposing views side by side. Computer control (C) is mentioned in an earlier sentence. The writer does not judge the critics (D).

questions.q: According to paragraph B, commercial vertical farming became possible because
questions.evidence: LEDs are cooler and more efficient, allowing shelves to be stacked closely together. This single development made commercial vertical farming possible
questions.explanation: "Stacked closely together" = "close layers". Hydroponics (A) and glasshouses (B) existed earlier and are not credited as the key change.

questions.q: How do vertical farms save water?
questions.evidence: water in a hydroponic system is collected and reused rather than soaking into the ground
questions.explanation: "Collected and reused" = "reuse". Rainwater (C) and seasonal growing (D) are not mentioned. The figure of ninety per cent describes the size of the saving, not how it is achieved.

questions.q: Which advantage of locating vertical farms near cities is mentioned?
questions.evidence: vertical farms can deliver produce to shops within hours of harvest
questions.explanation: "Within hours" = "quickly". Workers (A) and land prices (B) are not mentioned. Cheaper electricity (D) is linked to night-time use in Paragraph E, not to city locations.

questions.q: Why are staple crops such as wheat not grown in vertical farms?
questions.evidence: the electricity needed to light a field's worth of wheat indoors would make the resulting bread far too expensive
questions.explanation: The obstacle is the cost of lighting. A is not stated, since the passage never says hydroponics cannot grow wheat. C and D are not mentioned.

questions.q: What does the writer say about the environmental impact of vertical farming?
questions.evidence: The overall environmental effect ... depends heavily on where the farm's energy comes from
questions.explanation: "Depends heavily" = "depends largely". A and D are too absolute: the passage says a lettuce may produce more emissions, which is not proof.

questions.q: Which statement best summarises the writer's conclusion?
questions.evidence: not as a replacement for conventional agriculture but as an addition to it ... vertical farms may simply help to fill some of the gaps
questions.explanation: "An addition" and "fill some of the gaps" = "a limited supporting role". A is directly contradicted. C narrows one example (harsh climates) too far, and D overstates the business closures described in Paragraph E.

lesson.title: "Choose TWO letters" questions
lesson.text: In a Choose TWO question, treat each of the five options as a separate True/False check against the passage. Usually two options are clearly supported, and the other three are unsupported, contradicted, or attributed to the wrong time or group. Do not choose an option just because it sounds reasonable. Each correct option must be stated in the passage. The two letters can be written in either order.
lesson.example: Passage: "Volunteers repaired the fence and planted trees; they did not have time to paint the shed." Which TWO things did the volunteers do? A repaired the fence ✓ B painted the shed ✗ C planted trees ✓ D built a shed ✗ E cut the grass ✗ (not mentioned).

questions.q: In the twentieth century, some families were advised to
questions.evidence: Some families who spoke a minority language at home were even encouraged to abandon it
questions.explanation: "Abandon" = "stop using". C is the opposite of the advice given at the time. Intelligence tests (D) appear in Paragraph B, but as a research method, not as advice to families.

questions.q: According to paragraph B, early studies of bilingual children were unreliable partly because
questions.evidence: The tests were usually given only in the majority language
questions.explanation: "Only in the majority language" = "in only one language". The other problem mentioned is family income, not sample size (A) or the children's age (C).

questions.q: How do researchers now view code-mixing in young children?
questions.evidence: Young bilingual children mix words mainly when they do not yet know a word ... linguists regard this as a normal and skilful use
questions.explanation: Option C combines both points. A is the old interpretation. D is contradicted, because the passage says adults mix languages "too".

questions.q: What does the writer say about bilingual children's vocabulary?
questions.evidence: when the words they know in both languages are counted together, their total vocabulary is usually similar to ... that of monolingual children
questions.explanation: "Counted together ... similar" = "combined size ... comparable". A contradicts this. B confuses combined vocabulary with vocabulary in each language, where bilingual children often know fewer words.

questions.q: According to paragraph E, what matters most in raising a bilingual child?
questions.evidence: the particular method matters less than the amount and variety of exposure a child receives
questions.explanation: "Amount and variety of exposure" = "how much varied contact". A is a word-match trap: the method is mentioned but is said to matter less. B and D are not mentioned.

questions.q: Which TWO of the following statements about bilingualism are supported by the passage?
questions.evidence:
if they sense that one of their languages is not valued, they may start refusing to speak it
The old advice to abandon a home language is now regarded as mistaken
questions.explanation: A is contradicted by "others ... have failed to find them" in Paragraph F. C is never stated. E is contradicted by "Adult bilinguals mix languages too" in Paragraph C.

lesson.title: Reason and cause questions
lesson.text: Questions beginning Why ...? or containing because, the reason, led to or as a result test cause and effect. In the passage, look for linking language such as because, since, as, so, therefore, this means that, due to. Make sure the option gives the cause of the specific effect in the question. A passage often lists several causes for different effects, and distractors borrow a real cause from the wrong effect.
lesson.example:
Passage: "The library closed early because of staff shortages; it also stopped lending DVDs, since few people borrowed them." Why did the library stop lending DVDs?
Answer: low demand. Trap: staff shortages, which is the cause of a different change.

questions.q: What does the writer say about natural history museums?
questions.evidence: for some natural history museums, which may hold millions of ... specimens, the proportion is far smaller
questions.explanation: The "far smaller" proportion refers to the share of the collection on display. A is the opposite. The passage says stores are often in a separate building, so C is wrong.

questions.q: According to paragraph B, curators choose only some objects for display because
questions.evidence: A museum that attempted to display everything would produce galleries so crowded that visitors would struggle to notice anything
questions.explanation: "So crowded ... struggle to notice anything" = "confusing". A, B and D are not given as reasons.

questions.q: Why are some textiles and paper documents displayed for only short periods?
questions.evidence: Textiles, watercolours, photographs and documents on paper fade ... and the damage cannot be reversed
questions.explanation: "Cannot be reversed" = "permanently". Lending (A) is mentioned in Paragraph E, but not as a reason for short display periods.

questions.q: Why is it important to keep temperature and humidity stable in stores?
questions.evidence: rapid changes cause materials such as wood and ivory to expand and shrink, eventually cracking
questions.explanation: Pests (B) are dealt with separately, using traps and inspections. Comfort (A) and cost (D) are not mentioned in relation to stable conditions.

questions.q: The example of the preserved birds is used to show that stored objects
questions.evidence: Researchers ... visit museum stores to examine specimens; a single collection of preserved birds ... may allow scientists to measure how the size of a species has changed
questions.explanation: The birds illustrate research use. Lending (D) is a separate point in the same paragraph, so it is a distractor from the wrong sentence.

questions.q: What does the writer say about digitising collections?
questions.evidence: This digitisation is slow and costly ... Nevertheless, it allows people who could never visit in person to explore collections
questions.explanation: "Costly" = "expensive", and "people who could never visit ... explore collections" = "widens access". A and D are contradicted by "slow" and "decades".

questions.q: In the final paragraph, the writer compares museum stores to libraries in order to
questions.evidence: they are closer to libraries: organised, protected and constantly consulted
questions.explanation: "Organised, protected" = "well managed", and "constantly consulted" = "regularly used". The other options are not supported by the paragraph.

lesson.title: Inference questions ("suggests", "implies", "can be inferred")
lesson.text: An inference question asks for something the passage does not say in one sentence but makes clearly true when you combine the information. A correct inference is a small, safe step from the text. It is never a guess, a general-knowledge fact, or an exaggeration. To test an option, ask: "If the passage is true, must this also be true?" If the answer is only "possibly", reject it. Strong distractors in inference questions are often reasonable-sounding ideas that the passage never supports, or that go one step too far.
lesson.example:
Passage: "The shop's winter sales fell every year until it began delivering to customers' homes; since then, winter has become its busiest season." What can be inferred?
Correct: delivery helped the shop overcome a seasonal problem. Too far: home delivery is the best strategy for all shops.

questions.q: According to paragraph A, what makes tree rings especially useful for dating?
questions.evidence: Their width varies from year to year according to growing conditions ... It is this variation, rather than the rings themselves, that has made tree rings one of the most precise dating tools
questions.explanation: The writer explicitly locates the usefulness in the variation. C describes how a single ring forms but is not the reason for its usefulness. D is related to the rainfall point but is not stated.

questions.q: What can be inferred about Douglass from paragraph B?
questions.evidence: Douglass was not originally interested in archaeology at all. He hoped that tree rings might preserve a record of past climate
questions.explanation: His dating method grew out of climate research, which is a different aim. A reverses his background: he was an astronomer. C goes too far, because he only "hoped" to find evidence. D is not stated.

questions.q: In paragraph B, the writer compares a sequence of rings to a barcode in order to show that
questions.evidence: A particular run of narrow rings ... appeared in tree after tree, like a barcode
questions.explanation: The comparison stresses a distinctive, repeatable pattern that can be matched, which leads directly into cross-dating in Paragraph C. B is too extreme, because trees are said to share patterns "from the same area", not worldwide.

questions.q: Why was the beam found in 1929 so important?
questions.evidence: they could not at first be connected to the chronology built from living trees ... a single charred beam ... contained rings that overlapped with both
questions.explanation: "Overlapped with both" = "linked". B is a trap based on the word "charred". D is contradicted, because the settlements had been dated "only by estimate" and could now be given precise years.

questions.q: What does the writer suggest about radiocarbon dating?
questions.evidence: results that must be corrected ... Tree rings of known age provide the reference against which those corrections are made
questions.explanation: Radiocarbon dating relies on tree rings for correction. A goes beyond the passage. C reverses the comparison, since tree rings are the more precise method.

questions.q: If a beam has lost its outer layers, researchers can
questions.evidence: researchers can give only the earliest possible felling date, not the actual one
questions.explanation: This is a direct paraphrase. B combines two separate limitations incorrectly. D applies only to timber "with its outermost ring intact" (Paragraph E).

questions.q: What is the main point of paragraph G?
questions.evidence: Archaeologists therefore treat a tree-ring date as a precise statement about a tree, not automatically about a building ... Interpreted with that caution
questions.explanation: The paragraph urges caution when linking a tree's date to a structure. B contradicts the praise that follows. C reverses the point about reused timber, which may make wood older than the building.

lesson.title: Whose opinion is it?
lesson.text:
At Medium level, passages often contain several voices: designers, companies, researchers, critics and the writer. Questions may ask what one particular group believed or what the writer thinks. A common distractor states an opinion that really appears in the passage but belongs to someone else.

Before answering, identify the speaker in the question stem, then find that speaker in the passage. Useful clues: according to X, X argued, critics claim, it is often said (not necessarily the writer's view), and in my view, arguably, it seems clear, the real problem is (often the writer's view).
lesson.example:
Passage: "Many parents believe homework builds discipline. The evidence, however, suggests its value depends largely on the child's age." What is the writer's view?
Correct: the benefits of homework vary with age. Trap: homework builds discipline, which is the parents' belief.

questions.q: What point does the writer make in paragraph A?
questions.evidence: the open-plan office was not originally conceived as a way of saving money, which is how many employees now regard it
questions.explanation: This sets employees' current view against the original purpose. A states the employees' view as if it were the historical fact. C reverses the trend. D is contradicted by "widely resented".

questions.q: The designers of the Bürolandschaft believed that
questions.evidence: The designers believed that hierarchy was built into the architecture of traditional offices
questions.explanation: "Hierarchy built into the architecture" = "design reinforced differences in status". Plants (A) are only a design detail. C and D describe the arrangements the designers were rejecting.

questions.q: What does paragraph C suggest about Robert Propst's system?
questions.evidence: highly successful commercially, but not in the way he had intended ... Propst himself later expressed deep regret
questions.explanation: Companies used the system to create cubicles, which went against his aims. A is contradicted by "highly successful commercially". B describes how companies used the system, not what it was designed for.

questions.q: According to paragraph D, which reason for open offices do companies present as more practical than idealistic?
questions.evidence: Companies also point out, less idealistically, that open offices are cheaper
questions.explanation: The signal "less idealistically" marks the practical argument. A, B and D are the idealistic claims made by supporters.

questions.q: What was unexpected about the results of the badge study?
questions.evidence: Contrary to expectations, face-to-face interaction fell sharply after the move
questions.explanation: "Contrary to expectations" identifies what was unexpected. B reverses the finding, since electronic messages increased. D is not stated and is unlikely given the headphone detail.

questions.q: What does the writer say about the link between open offices and stress?
questions.evidence: some studies have linked open-plan environments with higher levels of reported stress ... although the causes of these patterns are difficult to separate from other features of the workplace
questions.explanation: A link exists, but its cause is uncertain. A overstates the finding and B contradicts it. D confuses stress with the separate point that concentration tasks "suffer most".

questions.q: What is the writer's overall view?
questions.evidence: what has usually been lost is not walls but choice. An office in which people can move away from noise ... and come together ... is likely to serve them better
questions.explanation: The writer argues for choice between different spaces. A is rejected in "either a corridor of closed doors". B is contradicted by the conditions described in Paragraph G. D conflicts with the writer's respect for the original designers.

title: The Bridge That Would Not Keep Still

lesson.title: Explanations of processes
lesson.text:
Some passages explain how something happens through a chain of causes (A leads to B, which strengthens A...). Questions may test one link in the chain or the chain as a whole. Distractors often present the right elements in the wrong order, or they describe the trigger as if it were the whole explanation.

Before looking at the options, write the chain yourself in three or four short notes (for example: small sway → walkers adjust step → push in time → bigger sway). Then choose the option that matches your notes.
lesson.example: Passage: "As more cars joined the road, traffic slowed; slower traffic made drivers brake sharply, which slowed it further." Why did the traffic keep slowing? Correct: drivers' reactions made the slowdown worse. Trap: there were too many cars, which is only the starting point.

questions.q: What does the writer say about the response of newspapers?
questions.evidence: many assumed that its designers had made an elementary mistake. The truth was more interesting
questions.explanation: The writer presents the newspapers' view as a mistaken assumption. A is the opposite. The closure is not linked to newspapers (C), and the figure of 90,000 is the writer's own estimate (D).

questions.q: According to paragraph B, the bridge was closed because
questions.evidence: What the designers had not anticipated was a particular interaction between the structure and the people walking on it
questions.explanation: "Not anticipated" = "unexpected". A and B are contradicted by "structurally safe". D is wrong, because the passage identifies sideways forces, not vertical ones, as the problem.

questions.q: Why do sideways forces from walkers normally cause no problem?
questions.evidence: these small sideways forces are random: different walkers step at different moments, and the pushes cancel one another out
questions.explanation: This is a direct paraphrase. A sounds logical but is not stated. D is contradicted: the passage does not say bridges are designed to move with walkers.

questions.q: Which sequence best describes the process explained in paragraph C?
questions.evidence: If the deck begins to move even slightly ... people instinctively adjust their walking ... their sideways pushes start to occur in step with the sway, so that ... they reinforce it
questions.explanation: B gives the correct order. A reverses cause and effect. C refers to vertical bending, which is not described. D contradicts the reinforcing cycle.

questions.q: What did the tests with volunteers reveal?
questions.evidence: the sway remained small until the number of walkers passed a particular level. Beyond that point, the movement increased suddenly
questions.explanation: The movement began suddenly after a threshold was reached. A is directly contradicted by "does not happen gradually". C and D are not supported.

questions.q: What does paragraph E suggest about earlier cases of swaying bridges?
questions.evidence: described only briefly, in reports that received little attention ... never been brought together into a general understanding of the problem
questions.explanation: The earlier cases were not recognised as a general problem. D is contradicted by the mention of road bridges. B confuses these earlier cases with the rule changes that followed the London bridge (Paragraph G).

questions.q: Why did the engineers choose dampers rather than stiffening the bridge?
questions.evidence: Rather than stiffening the entire structure, which would have spoiled its slender design and required major reconstruction
questions.explanation: Dampers preserved the slender design. A wrongly introduces vertical movement. B and D are not stated: the passage never compares the cost of the two options.

lesson.title: "Why does the writer mention ...?"
lesson.text:
Some questions ask about the function of a detail: an example, a statistic, a comparison or a case study. The answer is not what the detail says but why it is there. Look at the sentence just before the detail, which is often the general claim, and ask: What point does this example prove or illustrate?

A frequent distractor simply restates the content of the example itself. That option is true, but it does not answer the question about purpose.
lesson.example: Passage: "Small habits can have large effects. A person who saves just two dollars a day will have over seven hundred dollars after a year." Why does the writer mention two dollars a day? Correct: to illustrate that small habits add up. Trap: to recommend a specific saving amount.

questions.q: In paragraph A, the writer defines light pollution as artificial light that is
questions.evidence: artificial light that is excessive, badly directed or present where and when it is not needed
questions.explanation: "Badly directed" = "poorly controlled", and "not needed" = "unnecessary". D uses the satellite detail from the same paragraph, but that detail is not part of the definition.

questions.q: Why does the writer mention professional observatories in paragraph B?
questions.evidence: Astronomers were the first to complain; professional observatories have repeatedly been forced to move
questions.explanation: The observatories illustrate how early astronomers were affected. D goes too far: observatories moved, but astronomy did not stop. B and C are not supported.

questions.q: Why does the writer describe the behaviour of newly hatched sea turtles?
questions.evidence: Many animals depend on natural patterns of light ... hatchlings may crawl inland instead
questions.explanation: The turtles are an example of the general claim that animals relying on natural light are misled. D overstates "many die". Hotel policy (C) is not discussed. The paragraph does not compare turtles with birds (A).

questions.q: What does the writer say about the effect of outdoor lighting on human sleep?
questions.evidence: Researchers are still investigating how far outdoor lighting, as opposed to screens and indoor lamps, contributes to such effects
questions.explanation: "Still investigating how far" = "exact contribution not yet clear". A and D overstate the evidence. B is not stated.

questions.q: What was unexpected about the introduction of LED streetlights?
questions.evidence: the switch was widely expected to reduce light pollution ... Elsewhere ... the amount of light emitted actually increased
questions.explanation: The result went against expectations. A is contradicted by "use far less electricity". D is contradicted by "can be directed more precisely".

questions.q: According to paragraph F, one advantage of tackling light pollution is that
questions.evidence: Unlike most forms of pollution, light pollution can be reduced almost instantly, and often at low cost
questions.explanation: "Almost instantly" = "quickly". B contradicts the simple methods listed. C and D are not stated: dark sky towns attract visitors, but nothing is said about crime or universal support.

questions.q: What is the writer's main point in paragraph G?
questions.evidence: The obstacle is less technical than psychological. Light is widely associated with safety and progress
questions.explanation: The key challenge is people's attitudes. A is contradicted by "not to return cities to darkness". B is contradicted by "surprisingly mixed". Glare (D) is only one supporting point.

lesson.title: Timing and conditions
lesson.text:
Research passages often report that a result appears only under certain conditions: after a delay, in one group, or when a task is difficult. Medium-level distractors ignore these conditions and state the result as if it were always true.

When a stem mentions a time or condition (immediately, after a week, when students..., at first), locate that exact condition in the passage. Then check whether the option keeps the condition or quietly drops it.
lesson.example: Passage: "The fertiliser increased growth, but only in sandy soils." What did the study find? Correct: the fertiliser helped plants in certain soils. Trap: the fertiliser increased plant growth, which drops the condition.

questions.q: According to paragraph A, students like rereading because it
questions.evidence: familiarity creates a comfortable sense of understanding
questions.explanation: "A comfortable sense of understanding" = "a feeling that they understand". C is contradicted by the research. D describes recall, not rereading.

questions.q: What does the writer say about attitudes to tests in education before the 2000s?
questions.evidence: tests were seen almost entirely as a way of measuring learning, not as a way of producing it
questions.explanation: "Measuring learning" = "assessment". D is contradicted: psychologists had noticed the effect early in the twentieth century. B reverses the attitude.

questions.q: In the experiments described in paragraph C, the rereading group
questions.evidence: tested five minutes later, the group that had spent more time rereading performed slightly better ... a week later, the result was reversed
questions.explanation: This is the time condition. A and B each ignore one of the two tests. D contradicts "had forgotten much".

questions.q: What surprised researchers about the students' predictions?
questions.evidence: the rereading group was more confident than the recall group
questions.explanation: The rereading group learned less (Paragraph C) but was more confident. A is too extreme. C is contradicted by the "mismatch" described.

questions.q: According to paragraph E, retrieval practice is most beneficial when
questions.evidence: greatest when practice is spread out over time ... and when learners check their answers afterwards
questions.explanation: Both conditions are in C. A reverses the first condition and B reverses the second. D misreads the path analogy, which is only a comparison.

questions.q: Why have some researchers suggested using the term "retrieval practice"?
questions.evidence: High-stakes tests, which may produce anxiety ... Some researchers have therefore suggested replacing the word 'testing' with 'retrieval practice', to make clear that the goal is learning rather than assessment
questions.explanation: The new term separates the method from stressful assessment. D is contradicted by "None of this means that schools should simply give students more examinations".

questions.q: Which of the following best summarises the idea of "desirable difficulty"?
questions.evidence: methods that demand effort ... tend to produce knowledge that lasts
questions.explanation: This is the core idea. A concerns difficult subjects, not methods. B is too absolute. D reverses the final sentence.

title: The Box That Changed the World

lesson.title: When the question and the passage share no words
lesson.text:
As difficulty rises, question stems use almost none of the passage's vocabulary. For example, a stem may say "workers' reaction" where the passage says "dockers' unions ... strikes". You cannot find the answer by scanning for matching words. Instead:

1. Turn the stem into a simple idea ("How did the workers feel?").

2. Use the question order and paragraph topics to find the right section.

3. Look for synonyms, examples or descriptions of the idea, not the same words. The option that repeats passage wording most closely is often the trap.
lesson.example: Stem: "How did residents respond to the new airport?" Passage: "Petitions were signed by thousands living nearby, and weekly protests continued for a year." Answer idea: strong opposition. No words are shared, but the meaning matches.

questions.q: What does paragraph A suggest about the shipping industry before containers?
questions.evidence: the cost of handling cargo at the docks was often greater than the cost of carrying it across the ocean
questions.explanation: Handling in port was often the larger cost. A reverses the comparison. D contradicts "Theft was also common".

questions.q: What point does the writer make about McLean's 1956 voyage?
questions.evidence: The cost of loading ... was a small fraction of what traditional methods would have required
questions.explanation: "A small fraction" = "greatly cut costs". A is contradicted by "Versions of this idea had been tried before". McLean owned a private company, so D is wrong.

questions.q: According to paragraph C, why were the early years of containerisation difficult?
questions.evidence: Without all these elements, containers offered little advantage ... investing in any one part of the system seemed risky until the others were in place
questions.explanation: This describes mutual dependence between parts of the system. A, C and D are not stated.

questions.q: What was the main significance of the international agreements of the 1960s?
questions.evidence: Standardisation allowed containers to move freely between shipping lines, ports and countries
questions.explanation: "Move freely between" = "interchangeable". B, C and D are not effects of the agreements described.

questions.q: How did many traditional city-centre ports respond to containerisation?
questions.evidence: lacked the space ... Traffic shifted to new facilities ... waterfront areas ... became largely empty
questions.explanation: The old ports could not adapt and lost activity. A and C are the opposite. D is not mentioned.

questions.q: How did dock workers react to the introduction of containers?
questions.evidence: Unions resisted ... accompanied in several countries by long and bitter disputes
questions.explanation: "Resisted" and "long ... disputes" = "opposed ... for long periods". The stem shares no words with the passage, so this answer depends on paraphrase. D is a trap built from "crane operators".

questions.q: What is the writer's main purpose in the final paragraph?
questions.evidence: technical inventions often matter less on their own than the systems, agreements and changes in organisation that allow them to be used
questions.explanation: The paragraph ends on a general lesson. D is a trap, because the lesson actually downplays individual invention.

lesson.title: Options that are "true but incomplete"
lesson.text: At Medium level, two options can both look correct. Often one of them is true but covers only part of what the question asks, or only part of the evidence. Compare the two final candidates against the whole relevant sentence or paragraph. The correct option usually summarises the full point, while the distractor captures only one detail of it.
lesson.example: Passage: "The village was abandoned because the river dried up and the new road bypassed it." Why was the village abandoned? A the river dried up (true but incomplete). B it lost both its water supply and its transport connection (complete). If only one letter is allowed, choose B.

questions.q: The writer describes the two farmers in paragraph A in order to show that
questions.evidence: more than a kilometre away ... They are having a conversation, using a whistled form of their ordinary spoken language
questions.explanation: The scene shows real conversation over distance. A is rejected directly ("not ... simple signals like those used to call a dog"). D is contradicted by the list of countries.

questions.q: According to paragraph B, a whistled language is best described as
questions.evidence: not an independent language ... It is a way of transposing an existing spoken language into whistles
questions.explanation: "Transposing" = "converting". A is denied directly. D misreads the "missing letters" comparison, which is only an analogy.

questions.q: What does paragraph C say about whistled forms of languages such as Spanish and Turkish?
questions.evidence: In languages like Spanish or Turkish ... whistlers instead imitate the qualities of vowels and consonants
questions.explanation: A describes languages where pitch distinguishes words. C is contradicted by "may therefore differ considerably between regions".

questions.q: Why are whistled languages found mainly in mountains and forests?
questions.evidence: where people live and work far apart and where travelling between them is slow. A whistle carries much further than a shout
questions.explanation: B combines both parts of the explanation. An option giving only one part would be incomplete. A and C are not stated. D reverses the point: whistles stand out from background noise.

questions.q: What does the writer say about Silbo Gomero today?
questions.evidence: a compulsory subject in the island's schools ... many schoolchildren ... can whistle, although relatively few use it in everyday life
questions.explanation: C captures both halves of the final sentence. A contradicts "relatively few". D describes where the practice survived elsewhere, not La Gomera.

questions.q: What did the research with speakers of whistled Turkish suggest?
questions.evidence: the brain's division of labour for language may be more flexible ... and that it depends partly on the physical form in which language reaches the ear
questions.explanation: This is a paraphrase of the finding. A contradicts "both halves". C and D are not stated.

questions.q: According to paragraph G, what do whistled languages reveal to linguists?
questions.evidence: shows how much of ordinary speech is redundant
questions.explanation: "Redundant" = "more information than listeners need". D is the opposite. C is not mentioned.

lesson.title: Questions about change over time
lesson.text: Passages about policies or developments often describe a before, a during and an after. Questions may ask how something changed, for example public opinion or traffic levels. Distractors frequently describe the correct situation at the wrong stage (what people thought before instead of after). Mark the time signals in the passage (initially, at first, during the trial, once, subsequently, by the end) and match each fact to its stage.
lesson.example: Passage: "At first, most residents opposed the new park; after it opened, surveys showed strong approval." How did opinion develop? Correct: it moved from opposition to support. Trap: most residents opposed the park, which is true, but only of the first stage.

questions.q: What did transport economists conclude about building new roads?
questions.evidence: new roads filled with traffic almost as soon as they opened, as people who had previously avoided driving ... began to do so
questions.explanation: New roads attract new traffic. A is the belief that economists rejected. C and D are not stated.

questions.q: According to paragraph B, the economists' argument was based on the idea that
questions.evidence: Each additional car slows down all the others, but the driver does not bear that cost
questions.explanation: This is a direct paraphrase. A, C and D are not part of the argument.

questions.q: What was the main innovation of later schemes such as London's?
questions.evidence: used cameras to record vehicle number plates automatically, making it possible to charge drivers without toll booths or permits
questions.explanation: The cameras replaced permits and booths. A, B and D are not mentioned.

questions.q: How did public opinion in Stockholm change?
questions.evidence: "a clear majority of residents opposed it" (Paragraph D) ... "By the time of the referendum, a majority of voters ... supported keeping the charge" (Paragraph E)
questions.explanation: This answer requires matching each fact to its stage. A reverses the direction. D is contradicted by the opinion polls mentioned in Paragraph D.

questions.q: What does the writer say about the fall in traffic during the trial?
questions.evidence: traffic ... fell by around a fifth – a larger reduction than many planners had predicted
questions.explanation: "Larger than predicted" = "exceeded predictions". A is the opposite. D contradicts "Journey times became shorter".

questions.q: According to researchers, a key reason for the change in Stockholm residents' views was that
questions.evidence: the fears that had dominated public debate ... largely failed to materialise
questions.explanation: "Failed to materialise" = "did not happen". D is one of the fears that did not happen. B goes beyond the passage, which says only that the feared loss of customers did not occur.

questions.q: What is the writer's position in paragraph G?
questions.evidence: How these arguments balance out depends heavily on how a particular scheme is designed and how its revenue is spent
questions.explanation: The writer takes a conditional position. A presents the critics' view as absolute. D is contradicted by "not a solution for every city".

lesson.title: Hard Multiple Choice — precise claims and the writer's qualified position
lesson.text:
At Hard level:

Every option may contain passage language. You must judge the strength and scope of each claim (some / most / all, may / does, in certain conditions / generally). The writer often takes a qualified position. They accept part of an argument and reject part of it. The correct option reflects that balance. Distractors state one side too strongly.

Evidence may be spread across paragraphs. A question about "the later research" may need information from two places.

Strategy: for each option, underline its claim word (e.g. proved, always, no effect, depends) and check whether the passage supports that exact strength.
lesson.example: Passage: "The drug helped some patients, but in larger trials the average benefit was close to zero, although certain groups still seemed to respond." Best summary: the drug's benefit appears limited to particular groups. Too strong: the drug does not work. Also too strong: the drug is effective.

questions.q: What does the writer suggest about the jam study's results in paragraph A?
questions.evidence: The larger display attracted more visitors, who stopped to look and taste. But when it came to buying, the result was reversed
questions.explanation: The large display attracted more interest but produced fewer sales. A reverses the visitor finding. D contradicts the sales difference.

questions.q: Why was the jam study considered surprising?
questions.evidence: it contradicted a principle that had seemed almost self-evident ... that people are better off with more options
questions.explanation: "Seemed almost self-evident" = "widely accepted assumption". A is a detail of the setting, not the reason the result was surprising.

questions.q: What does the writer imply about the way choice overload was used in paragraph B?
questions.evidence: cited in books, business advice and even government policy documents ... simplifying everything from pension plans to product ranges
questions.explanation: The word "even" and the range from pensions to products show how far the idea spread beyond its original evidence. This is an inference, and it is supported by the writer's later warning in Paragraph G. C is a trap: pensions were a policy target, not a source of evidence.

questions.q: What did the combined analysis described in paragraph D find?
questions.evidence: the average size of the choice-overload effect was close to zero
questions.explanation: "Close to zero" = "negligible". B turns "a few found" into "always". D is not supported, and Paragraph G says the result "may well have been genuine".

questions.q: Why does the writer think the conclusion in paragraph D "may have been premature"?
questions.evidence: An average close to zero does not necessarily mean that an effect never occurs; it can also arise when an effect is strong in some situations and absent or reversed in others
questions.explanation: This is the writer's stated reason. C is contradicted: the combined analysis included "published and unpublished experiments". D is not stated.

questions.q: According to paragraph E, large assortments are LEAST likely to cause difficulties when
questions.evidence: When shoppers already knew what they wanted ... large assortments caused few problems
questions.explanation: "Already knew what they wanted" = "clear preferences beforehand". A, B and D are the conditions under which large assortments are more likely to cause problems. This question tests careful reading of the direction of each condition.

questions.q: Which of the following best reflects the writer's view in paragraph G?
questions.evidence: The difficulty lies in treating a finding from one setting as a general law of human behaviour
questions.explanation: This matches C. A is denied: "The problem is rarely that the original researchers were wrong". D is too strong for the writer's conditional view. B is too extreme and is never stated.

title: The Puzzle of the First Farmers

lesson.title: Competing theories and how the evidence bears on them
lesson.text:
Hard passages often compare several explanations and then introduce evidence that affects them differently. Questions may ask which theory a finding challenges or what a discovery implies for an explanation. Build a quick grid in your head or on paper:

Theory Main claim Evidence for Evidence against

Then answer from the grid. Distractors frequently attach evidence to the wrong theory, or treat "challenges" as "disproves".
lesson.example: Passage: "Theory X says the lake dried because of farming; Theory Y blames a drought. Sediment shows the lake shrank before farms were built." What does the sediment suggest? Correct: it weakens Theory X. Traps: it proves Theory Y (too strong) and it supports Theory X (wrong direction).

questions.q: What is the writer's purpose in paragraph A?
questions.evidence: It is tempting ... to see its adoption as an obvious improvement ... Archaeological evidence suggests that the reality was far less straightforward
questions.explanation: The paragraph sets up an assumption in order to question it. A is too strong: the writer never calls farming a mistake. D is contradicted by "independently in several other parts of the world".

questions.q: What does the evidence from skeletons suggest about early farmers?
questions.evidence: the farmers were, on average, somewhat shorter ... more signs of poor nutrition, disease ... it did not obviously make individual lives easier or healthier
questions.explanation: C matches the careful strength of the claim ("no better, and often worse"). B reverses the claim about population, since farming allowed "populations to grow". D exaggerates: a failed harvest "could" bring hunger, not every year.

questions.q: According to the climate explanation in paragraph C, people began planting cereals because
questions.evidence: interrupted by a return to colder, drier conditions ... communities that had come to depend on abundant wild cereals began deliberately planting them when natural supplies declined
questions.explanation: The trigger is the decline in wild supplies. A is a trap: the warmer period explains why wild cereals spread, not why people began planting. C belongs to the first explanation.

questions.q: How does the social explanation differ from the other two explanations?
questions.evidence: places social life, rather than hunger, at the centre ... cultivation began as a way of supporting social and religious gatherings
questions.explanation: The social theory focuses on gatherings rather than hunger. A describes the other explanations. C is contradicted, because cereals are central to this view.

questions.q: Why is the dating of the site in Turkey significant?
questions.evidence: built ... before there is clear evidence of domesticated plants or animals in the region. The builders ... appear to have been hunter-gatherers
questions.explanation: The dates place the building before farming. A is the opposite. B is too strong: Paragraph F notes climate may have operated "at the same time". D is contradicted by the remains of wild animals.

questions.q: What does the writer consider the most secure conclusion that can be drawn from the site?
questions.evidence: What the site does make difficult to maintain is the older assumption that complex social organisation and monumental building could only follow the development of farming
questions.explanation: The writer separates contested interpretations from this firmer conclusion. A and D contradict the cautious view that "a single site ... cannot show what motivated communities across a large region". C is contradicted by the same paragraph.

questions.q: Which statement best reflects the view expressed in paragraph G?
questions.evidence: any single cause ... Farming arose independently in several regions ... the process in each seems to have been gradual
questions.explanation: C combines "gradual" with "different reasons". A reduces the explanation to one cause, which the writer rejects. B and D are contradicted by "gradual" and by the "long periods" in which people combined cultivation with hunting and gathering.

lesson.title: Counter-intuitive ideas
lesson.text: Some Hard passages explain an idea that goes against common sense. Here, for example, melting glaciers first increase the amount of water available and only later reduce it. Questions will test whether you have followed the argument precisely, and distractors will offer the "common-sense" version. When a passage signals surprise (paradoxically, counter-intuitively, at first sight, in fact), slow down and restate the idea in your own words before reading the options.
lesson.example: Passage: "Paradoxically, the new bypass increased traffic in the town centre, because it made the town easier to reach." Why did traffic increase? Correct: improved access attracted more visitors. Trap: the bypass sent traffic through the centre.

questions.q: Why does the writer describe glaciers as particularly important in regions such as the Andes?
questions.evidence: during the hottest and driest part of the year, precisely when rainfall is lowest and demand for water is highest
questions.explanation: The glaciers matter because of when their water arrives. A and C use absolute wording that the passage does not support. D is too extreme, since hydroelectric power is only one of several uses mentioned.

questions.q: According to paragraph B, why have summer river flows increased in many places?
questions.evidence: The extra meltwater is not new water but water drawn from a store that accumulated over centuries
questions.explanation: "Store that accumulated over centuries" = "stored over a long period". A is contradicted, because the glacier loses more than it gains. C is not mentioned.

questions.q: What causes meltwater to decline after peak water, even if warming continues?
questions.evidence: the area of ice exposed to summer warmth also shrinks, so that even if temperatures continue to rise, the total volume of meltwater eventually starts to fall
questions.explanation: Less exposed ice means less meltwater. A contradicts "temperatures continue to rise". C describes the situation after the glacier is gone, not the cause of the decline.

questions.q: What does the writer say about the timing of peak water?
questions.evidence: the answer varies greatly between regions ... a single global date for peak water is not meaningful
questions.explanation: A is directly rejected. B generalises from "some small, low-altitude glaciers". D is too strong, since models do give estimates.

questions.q: What is the main danger described in paragraph E?
questions.evidence: the temporary abundance will encourage people to become more reliant on it just before it diminishes
questions.explanation: This is the danger the writer identifies. A describes the future, not the current period of abundance. D is not stated.

questions.q: How do researchers respond to the argument that the importance of glaciers has been exaggerated?
questions.evidence: Researchers generally accept this point, but argue that annual totals can be misleading ... concentrated in particular seasons and in years of drought
questions.explanation: The researchers accept the figures but add a qualification. A and B misrepresent this in opposite directions. D is not stated.

questions.q: What is the central lesson of the passage, according to the final paragraph?
questions.evidence: present conditions can be a poor guide to the future when they are being sustained by a resource that is steadily being used up
questions.explanation: A is a direct paraphrase. B is contradicted by "None of this implies that nothing can be done". C overstates the role of reservoirs. D is the approach the writer warns against.

lesson.title: Technical explanations without technical knowledge
lesson.text:
Hard passages sometimes explain an engineering or scientific principle. You are not expected to know the subject; everything you need is in the text. Distractors in such passages often: sound technically plausible but are not stated, which is an outside-knowledge trap; confuse two related forces or components;

reverse the direction of a relationship (taller walls → more outward push, not less). Paraphrase each technical sentence into plain language as you read, for example: "the roof pushes the walls outward".
lesson.example: Passage: "The heavier the load on an arch, the more strongly it pushes sideways against its supports." Which is true? Correct: increasing the load increases sideways force. Trap: heavier arches need no side support.

questions.q: What contrast does the writer describe in paragraph A?
questions.evidence: made almost entirely of stone, yet their interiors seem light, even weightless
questions.explanation: This is the "two apparently contradictory impressions". D is only implied later in the passage, and it is not the contrast described in Paragraph A.

questions.q: According to paragraph B, the outward thrust of an arch increases when
questions.evidence: the outward push ... becomes greater as the load increases and as the arch becomes flatter
questions.explanation: A and B reverse the two relationships. D confuses compression, which is a normal condition in stone, with the cause of thrust.

questions.q: Why did earlier churches have small windows?
questions.evidence: any large opening would weaken the wall at precisely the point where it needed to resist the vault
questions.explanation: This is the structural reason. A and C sound plausible but require outside knowledge, since the passage never mentions cost or religious preference.

questions.q: Which innovation is described as reducing thrust for a given height?
questions.evidence: Pointed arches ... produced less outward thrust for a given height
questions.explanation: Ribbed vaults concentrate loads (A) and flying buttresses carry thrust away (B). Neither is said to reduce thrust. The distractors confuse related components.

questions.q: What does the writer imply about the large windows of the later cathedrals?
questions.evidence: not a decoration added to a solid structure but a consequence of a structural system that had moved the work of support elsewhere
questions.explanation: This is an inference supported directly by the text. A is the view the writer rejects. B is contradicted by the system's stability.

questions.q: What does the writer say about the knowledge of medieval builders?
questions.evidence: They relied instead on geometrical rules ... and on accumulated experience ... Each failure added to the knowledge of the building trade
questions.explanation: The writer explicitly rejects both "modern theory" (A, D) and "pure luck" (B) with "Neither view appears to be correct".

questions.q: According to paragraph G, why might an old cathedral become unstable?
questions.evidence: changes that alter their geometry, such as the movement of foundations, which may push the lines of force outside the stone
questions.explanation: A is contradicted by "what matters is not the strength of the material". C is contradicted by "considerable margin of safety". D is not mentioned.

lesson.title: Correlation, causation and research design
lesson.text:
Many research passages distinguish between finding that two things occur together (correlation) and showing that one causes the other (causation). Hard questions test whether you notice the writer's caution. Distractors turn "is associated with" into "causes", or ignore a limitation the writer mentions.

Watch for signals of study design: compared, followed over time, randomly assigned, before and after. Watch also for the writer's caveats: this does not prove, cannot rule out, it is possible that.
lesson.example: Passage: "People who drink more coffee tend to live longer, but coffee drinkers may also differ in income and exercise." Correct conclusion: the link may be explained by other factors. Trap: coffee extends life.

questions.q: What question does the writer raise in paragraph A?
questions.evidence: if we no longer need to form mental maps, will we gradually lose the ability to do so?
questions.explanation: This is a direct paraphrase. A, C and D are not raised as questions.

questions.q: What was the limitation of the first study of taxi drivers?
questions.evidence: on its own it could not show that learning the streets had changed the drivers' brains ... people who already had a larger hippocampus were more likely to choose the job
questions.explanation: The problem is the direction of cause. B contradicts the finding. A and C are not stated.

questions.q: Why did the later study of trainee drivers provide stronger evidence?
questions.evidence: following trainee drivers over time. Brain scans taken before training ... After several years
questions.explanation: A before-and-after design strengthens the causal claim. C is contradicted: growth appeared only in trainees who qualified. D contradicts "showed no difference" before training.

questions.q: In the study described in paragraph D, which participants showed the greatest decline in spatial memory?
questions.evidence: those whose use of navigation apps had increased most showed the greatest decline
questions.explanation: This is stated directly. C is a trap built from the alternative explanation in Paragraph E, which the follow-up made "less likely".

questions.q: Which weakness of the app study does the writer mention in paragraph E?
questions.evidence: the study relied partly on participants' own reports of how often they used navigation apps
questions.explanation: "Participants' own reports" = "what participants said about their own behaviour". D reverses the other limitation: the study did not randomly assign participants.

questions.q: What does the writer say about the laboratory experiments in paragraph F?
questions.evidence: These results concern short-term effects of a single journey ... cannot on their own show that the habit ... produces lasting changes
questions.explanation: A turns this into proof of a lasting effect, which the writer denies. C contradicts the reported differences.

questions.q: Which statement best reflects the writer's conclusion?
questions.evidence: spatial memory ... responds to use ... apps could be designed to encourage rather than replace this effort
questions.explanation: A is explicitly rejected ("It would be wrong ... to conclude"). C is too extreme compared with "occasionally switch the app off". D contradicts "What the evidence does suggest".

lesson.title: When a famous story is revised
lesson.example: Passage: "The statue was long believed to be Roman. Recent tests suggest parts are Roman but the head was added in the eighteenth century." Best summary: the statue combines ancient and later parts. Traps: it is entirely Roman and it is an eighteenth-century fake.

questions.q: According to the popular account in paragraph A, the recovery of trees along rivers was
questions.evidence: By hunting elk ... the predators had allowed trees such as willow and aspen, which elk eat, to recover
questions.explanation: The wolves helped trees indirectly, by reducing elk. C reverses the sequence, since beavers came after the trees recovered. A is not supported.

questions.q: Why does the writer mention sea otters and kelp forests?
questions.evidence: cascades had been clearly demonstrated in some simpler systems, such as coastal waters where sea otters ...
questions.explanation: The otters show an established example of a cascade. D is contradicted by "on land". B confuses this paragraph with the later revision of the story.

questions.q: What made the "landscape of fear" idea especially attractive?
questions.evidence: plants in these places recovered even if elk numbers had not fallen much ... predators could reshape ecosystems through behaviour alone
questions.explanation: The idea's appeal was that fear alone could have effects. A contradicts "not fallen much". C contradicts Paragraph D, which says wolves hunt mainly around dawn, dusk and night.

questions.q: What did studies using satellite collars reveal about elk behaviour?
questions.evidence: elk did adjust their behaviour ... but mainly at certain times of day
questions.explanation: This captures both parts of the finding. A is contradicted by "little evidence that they abandoned such places". B is contradicted by "did adjust".

questions.q: Why does the writer list bears, mountain lions, human hunting and dry years in paragraph E?
questions.evidence: Distinguishing the contribution of wolves from these other influences is extremely difficult
questions.explanation: The list shows other possible causes, which makes the wolves' role hard to separate. A and C go further than the passage, since the writer never ranks or denies the wolves' effect (see Paragraph G). D contradicts "no controlled experiment is possible".

questions.q: According to paragraph F, why did willows sometimes fail to return even where browsing fell?
questions.evidence: even a large reduction in elk browsing did not necessarily allow willows to return, because the ground beside the streams had become too dry
questions.explanation: This is stated directly. A, C and D are not mentioned.

questions.q: What is the writer's overall conclusion about the Yellowstone story?
questions.evidence: None of this means that the wolves had no effect ... Restoring a missing species may be a necessary step ... but it is not always a sufficient one
questions.explanation: This is the qualified middle position. A and B are the two extremes the writer rejects. D is not stated and conflicts with "necessary step".

lesson.title: Numbers and dates
lesson.text: In easy sets, many statements contain a number, a date or a distance. Find that figure or a close equivalent in the passage (70,000 may appear as seventy thousand, and half as 50%). Then check what the number refers to. A statement can use the right number for the wrong thing (FALSE), or add a detail about the number that the passage never gives (NOT GIVEN).
lesson.example: Passage: "The tower is 90 metres tall." Statement: "The tower is 90 metres wide." → FALSE? No: the passage says nothing about width, so it is NOT GIVEN. It would be FALSE only if the passage gave a different width.

questions.q: An Arctic tern weighs more than a kilogram.
questions.evidence: weighing little more than a hundred grams
questions.explanation: A hundred grams is far less than a kilogram, so the passage contradicts the statement.

questions.q: Arctic terns usually return to the same nesting site every year.
questions.evidence: Paragraph B describes where terns nest ("in colonies on the ground, often on small islands or coastal gravel").
questions.explanation: The passage never says whether individual birds return to the same site each year, so the statement cannot be confirmed or contradicted.

questions.q: Adult terns may attack people who come close to their nests.
questions.evidence: diving at any intruder – including humans – and striking with their sharp beaks
questions.explanation: "Striking ... intruders including humans" = "may attack people".

questions.q: Before the tracking study, scientists had no evidence that Arctic terns travelled south.
questions.evidence: Scientists knew that terns ringed in the north were later found in the south
questions.explanation: Scientists already had evidence from ringed birds before the tracking study. What they lacked was information about the routes.

questions.q: The terns' routes between north and south were longer than a direct flight would be.
questions.evidence: These routes are much longer than the straight-line distance
questions.explanation: "Straight-line distance" = "direct flight".

questions.q: Terns rest for several weeks in the North Atlantic where there is plenty of food.
questions.evidence: The terns stop for several weeks in areas of the North Atlantic where food is plentiful
questions.explanation: "Stop" = "rest", and "plentiful" = "plenty of food".

questions.q: Arctic terns sleep while flying over the ocean.
questions.evidence: Paragraph E describes feeding while travelling, but the passage never mentions sleep.
questions.explanation: Nothing confirms or contradicts the statement.

questions.q: Arctic tern populations have declined in every region where they breed.
questions.evidence: Although the species is widespread, some populations have declined
questions.explanation: "Some" contradicts "every region". This is a qualifier trap. Note that it is FALSE, not NOT GIVEN, because "some populations have declined" means the decline is not universal.

lesson.title: "First", "only" and other strong words
lesson.text:
Statements often contain words that make a strong claim: first, only, never, always, all, the most. The passage may support the topic but not the strength of the claim.

If the passage says someone was among the first, a statement saying they were the first is usually NOT GIVEN. It would be FALSE only if the passage names someone earlier. If the passage says others had tried before, then a statement that X was the first to try is FALSE.
lesson.example: Passage: "Several companies had made electric cars before 1900." Statement: "The first electric car was made in 1920." → FALSE, because cars existed before 1900.

questions.q: Before Birdseye's work, meat and fish were already being frozen for transport.
questions.evidence: meat and fish were being frozen for transport over long distances
questions.explanation: This happened by the late nineteenth century, before Birdseye's work in the 1910s.

questions.q: In the early twentieth century, frozen food was generally considered to be of high quality.
questions.evidence: frozen food had a poor reputation ... suitable only for people who could afford nothing better
questions.explanation: "Poor reputation" contradicts "high quality".

questions.q: Birdseye was the first person to freeze fish.
questions.evidence: "Inuit fishermen preserved their catch ... fish ... froze almost instantly" (Paragraph B), and meat and fish were already being frozen commercially (Paragraph A)
questions.explanation: The passage shows that fish were frozen before Birdseye, which makes "the first" impossible.

questions.q: Birdseye worked in Labrador for more than ten years.
questions.evidence: spent several years working in Labrador
questions.explanation: "Several years" does not tell us whether the period was more or less than ten years. The passage neither confirms nor contradicts the statement.

questions.q: Slow freezing creates large ice crystals that damage food.
questions.evidence: When food freezes slowly, large ice crystals form inside it, breaking the walls of the cells
questions.explanation: "Breaking cell walls" = "damage food".

questions.q: Birdseye's first company was successful.
questions.evidence: His first business ... failed through lack of money
questions.explanation: "Failed" contradicts "successful".

questions.q: Frozen food first went on sale in Massachusetts in 1930.
questions.evidence: in 1929 Birdseye sold his business ... The following year, frozen vegetables ... went on sale in a group of shops in the state of Massachusetts
questions.explanation: "The following year" after 1929 = 1930. The passage describes this as the moment the products went on sale.

questions.q: Birdseye later regretted selling his business.
questions.evidence: Paragraph E states that he sold the business "for a considerable sum". His feelings about the sale are never mentioned.
questions.explanation: Nothing confirms or contradicts any regret.

lesson.title: Cause-and-effect statements
lesson.text:
A statement may connect two facts with because, so, led to, as a result. Check carefully: The passage gives the same cause → TRUE.

The passage gives a different cause, or says the connection does not exist → FALSE. The passage mentions both facts but gives no link between them → NOT GIVEN.
lesson.example: Passage: "The café changed its menu in May. Its sales rose in June." Statement: "Sales rose because of the new menu." → NOT GIVEN. Both events are mentioned, but no cause is stated.

questions.q: In the twentieth century, libraries offered reference books that many families could not afford.
questions.evidence: reference works such as encyclopaedias and dictionaries that most families could not afford to buy
questions.explanation: The statement says "many" and the passage says "most". Since most includes many, the statement is TRUE.

questions.q: Some commentators expected the internet to make libraries unnecessary.
questions.evidence: led many commentators to predict that libraries would soon become unnecessary
questions.explanation: "Predict" = "expected".

questions.q: Libraries were closed because too few people used them.
questions.evidence: local authorities under financial pressure reduced library opening hours, and some branches were closed
questions.explanation: The passage mentions financial pressure but does not say the closures were caused by low use. The cause in the statement is neither confirmed nor contradicted.

questions.q: In many areas, book lending has decreased.
questions.evidence: Book lending in many areas has fallen from its peak
questions.explanation: "Fallen" = "decreased".

questions.q: All government services can now be accessed only online.
questions.evidence: a growing number of essential services ... are now available mainly or only online
questions.explanation: "Mainly or only" shows that not all services are online-only, which contradicts "all".

questions.q: Libraries in some places lend musical instruments.
questions.evidence: Others lend items ... such as tools, musical instruments or cooking equipment
questions.explanation: "Others" means some libraries, which matches "some places".

questions.q: All regular library users support the recent changes.
questions.evidence: These changes have not been welcomed by everyone. Some regular users regret the loss of silence
questions.explanation: This directly contradicts "all ... support".

questions.q: New central libraries have attracted more visitors than old ones.
questions.evidence: New central libraries "have become popular public landmarks"
questions.explanation: No comparison of visitor numbers with older libraries is made.

lesson.title: Sequence and time words
lesson.text: Statements may test the order of events using before, after, later, until, at first, soon. Put the events from the passage on a simple timeline in the margin as you read. A statement that reverses the order is FALSE. A statement about timing that the passage does not settle, such as how long something lasted when only the start date is given, is NOT GIVEN.
lesson.example:
Passage: "The bridge opened in 1901; electric trams crossed it from 1910."
Statement: "Trams used the bridge from the day it opened." → FALSE, because the trams started nine years later.

questions.q: In the mid-nineteenth century, main-line railway stations were located in the centre of London.
questions.evidence: the main railway lines ... ended at stations on the edge of the central area
