questions.explanation: "On the edge" contradicts "in the centre".

questions.q: The idea of an underground railway was initially popular with the public.
questions.evidence: The idea was widely ridiculed at first
questions.explanation: "Ridiculed" is the opposite of "popular".

questions.q: Construction of the first line started in 1860.
questions.evidence: construction of the first line began in 1860
questions.explanation: "Began" = "started".

questions.q: The first underground line was built by a government department.
questions.evidence: The passage says the main railway lines were "built by separate private companies" (Paragraph A), but it never says who built the underground line.
questions.explanation: Nothing confirms or contradicts the statement. Do not assume the underground line was built the same way as the main lines.

questions.q: The first line was about six kilometres long.
questions.evidence: The line, about six kilometres long
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: No passengers complained about smoke on the first line.
questions.evidence: travellers still complained about the smoky and sulphurous air
questions.explanation: This contradicts "no passengers complained".

questions.q: The first deep-level line used electric trains.
questions.evidence: the first deep-level line ... was worked by electric trains
questions.explanation: "Worked by" = "used".

questions.q: The older sub-surface lines were converted to electric power before 1890.
questions.evidence: The first deep line with electric trains opened in 1890 (Paragraph E), and "in the early twentieth century the older sub-surface lines were also converted" (Paragraph F)
questions.explanation: The conversion happened after 1900, not before 1890, so the statement reverses the sequence.

title: A Short History of the Pencil

lesson.title: Don't let common sense answer for you
lesson.text: Some statements sound obviously true because of what you already know or expect. In TFNG, "sounds true" is not evidence. If you find yourself thinking "that must be right" but you cannot point to a sentence, the answer is probably NOT GIVEN. This trap is especially common with everyday topics.
lesson.example:
Passage: "The first bicycles had no pedals; riders pushed along with their feet."
Statement: "Early bicycles were uncomfortable to ride." It sounds likely, but nothing about comfort is stated → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: The basic design of the pencil has changed greatly over the last two centuries.
questions.evidence: the basic design has changed surprisingly little in more than two centuries
questions.explanation: "Changed surprisingly little" contradicts "changed greatly".

questions.q: Pencil "lead" is made from graphite rather than lead.
questions.evidence: the 'lead' in a pencil contains no lead at all. It is made from graphite
questions.explanation: This is a direct paraphrase.

questions.q: The graphite found in England was mixed with clay before use.
questions.evidence: The English graphite was so pure that it could be cut into thin sticks and used directly
questions.explanation: "Used directly" contradicts the idea that it was mixed with clay. Mixing with clay was Conté's later method for replacing English graphite.

questions.q: The English graphite mine was protected against theft.
questions.evidence: the mine was guarded to prevent theft
questions.explanation: "Guarded" = "protected".

questions.q: Conté had worked as a pencil maker before the government asked for his help.
questions.evidence: Conté is described only as "an engineer"
questions.explanation: His earlier work is not described. Being an engineer does not rule out previous pencil-making, so the statement is neither confirmed nor contradicted.

questions.q: Adding more clay to the mixture makes a pencil harder.
questions.evidence: More clay produced a harder pencil
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: Six-sided pencils were introduced to make them easier to hold.
questions.evidence: six-sided pencils "helped to stop them rolling off desks"
questions.explanation: The passage gives a different reason. Because it states the purpose, and that purpose differs from the one in the statement, the answer is FALSE. If no reason had been given at all, it would be NOT GIVEN. Common sense may suggest easier holding, but only the passage counts.

questions.q: Pencils are used more often than pens in schools today.
questions.evidence: Pencils "remain widely used" and are used by schoolchildren
questions.explanation: No comparison with pens in schools is made.

lesson.title: Partial matches
lesson.text:
A statement may be half right: one part matches the passage and the other part does not. Check every part of the statement.

If any part is contradicted → FALSE.

If one part is confirmed and another part is not mentioned → NOT GIVEN.

The answer is TRUE only when every part is supported.
lesson.example: Passage: "The river flows south and is used for irrigation." Statement: "The river flows south and is used for drinking water." The first part matches, but drinking water is not mentioned → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: The water of the Dead Sea is about ten times saltier than seawater.
questions.evidence: Its water is roughly ten times saltier than that of the ocean
questions.explanation: "Roughly" = "about", and "the ocean" = "seawater".

questions.q: Water leaves the Dead Sea through a river flowing south.
questions.evidence: The Dead Sea has no outlet ... leaves only by evaporation
questions.explanation: This contradicts the idea of a river carrying water out.

questions.q: The Dead Sea's level remained completely unchanged for thousands of years.
questions.evidence: although the level varied naturally, the lake remained broadly stable
questions.explanation: "Varied" contradicts "completely unchanged". This is a qualifier trap.

questions.q: Water from the Jordan is diverted for agriculture and drinking.
questions.evidence: divert water from the Jordan and its tributaries for drinking and agriculture
questions.explanation: This is a direct paraphrase.

questions.q: Mineral extraction at the southern end of the lake began before dams were built on the Jordan.
questions.evidence: Paragraph C describes the dams and Paragraph D describes mineral extraction, but no dates are given for either.
questions.explanation: The order of the two developments cannot be determined from the passage.

questions.q: The Dead Sea's surface has fallen by more than a metre per year and tourist numbers have fallen as a result.
questions.evidence: "falling by more than a metre per year" (Paragraph E) confirms the first part. Hotels are now far from the water, but tourist numbers are never mentioned.
questions.explanation: This is a partial match: one part is confirmed and the other is absent, so the whole statement is NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: Sinkholes form when fresh water dissolves underground salt.
questions.evidence: The fresh water dissolves the salt, creating underground cavities, and eventually the ground above collapses
questions.explanation: The process matches the statement.

questions.q: The Red Sea project has been approved and construction has begun.
questions.evidence: The project has been discussed for many years, but its future remains uncertain
questions.explanation: An "uncertain" future is incompatible with approval and construction having begun.

lesson.title: What was claimed vs what was found
lesson.text: Medium passages often separate what a study found, what others claimed it found, and what later research showed. A statement may describe a claim as if it were a finding. For example, "the study showed that music makes babies smarter" may be FALSE if the study tested only university students. Always ask: who says this, and on what evidence?
lesson.example: Passage: "The trial tested the drug on adults; newspapers reported it would help children." Statement: "The trial showed the drug helps children." → FALSE, because the trial involved only adults. (If the passage had not said who was tested, it would be NOT GIVEN.)

questions.q: In the 1993 experiment, students listened to Mozart for ten minutes.
questions.evidence: A group of university students listened for ten minutes to one of three things: a sonata by Mozart ...
questions.explanation: The students in the Mozart condition listened for ten minutes.

questions.q: The improvement in spatial reasoning lasted for several hours.
questions.evidence: it lasted only around ten to fifteen minutes
questions.explanation: This contradicts "several hours".

questions.q: The original researchers claimed that Mozart's music increased general intelligence.
questions.evidence: They did not suggest that listening to Mozart made people more intelligent in general
questions.explanation: This is a direct contradiction. The claim of general intelligence came from the media, not from the researchers.

questions.q: The students in the 1993 study were all studying music at university.
questions.evidence: The participants are described only as "university students"
questions.explanation: Their subjects of study are never mentioned, so the statement cannot be confirmed or contradicted.

questions.q: A free classical music recording was given to parents of newborn babies in one American state.
questions.evidence: the governor proposed that the parents of every newborn child should receive a free classical music recording, and the plan was put into practice
questions.explanation: "Put into practice" confirms the recordings were actually given, not just proposed.

questions.q: Sales of classical music recordings rose sharply after the study was published.
questions.evidence: Businesses began selling recordings ... marketed to parents
questions.explanation: The passage mentions that recordings were marketed but gives no sales figures or trends. Do not infer a rise in sales from the fact that recordings were marketed.

questions.q: The 1999 review found strong evidence of a Mozart effect.
questions.evidence: any benefit ... was very small and might not be real at all
questions.explanation: This contradicts "strong evidence".

questions.q: In one study, the difference between lively and sad music disappeared when mood and alertness were taken into account.
questions.evidence: when the researchers measured the students' mood and alertness, the difference between the two conditions disappeared
questions.explanation: The statement closely paraphrases this sentence.

questions.q: Research on learning a musical instrument has reached clear and agreed conclusions.
questions.evidence: its conclusions are still debated
questions.explanation: "Still debated" contradicts "clear and agreed".

lesson.title: NOT GIVEN when the topic is mentioned
lesson.text:
At Medium level, NOT GIVEN statements usually deal with a topic that the passage does discuss. For example, the passage discusses shopkeepers' fears, and the statement makes a specific claim about those shopkeepers that the passage never settles. Don't choose TRUE or

FALSE just because the topic appears. Ask: Does the passage decide this specific claim?
lesson.example: Passage: "Residents objected to the new bus lane, and the council held a public meeting." Statement: "The council changed its plans after the meeting." The meeting is mentioned, but its outcome is not → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: Most pedestrian streets in European city centres have been car-free for centuries.
questions.evidence: most were full of cars and buses until the second half of the twentieth century
questions.explanation: This contradicts "car-free for centuries".

questions.q: Copenhagen's main shopping street was closed to cars in 1962.
questions.evidence: In 1962, the city closed its main shopping street ... to motor traffic
questions.explanation: "Motor traffic" = "cars".

questions.q: Some shopkeepers in Copenhagen later admitted they had been wrong to oppose the scheme.
questions.evidence: Shopkeepers' fears are described (Paragraph B), and "many shops reported higher sales" (Paragraph C)
questions.explanation: The shopkeepers are discussed, but the passage never says whether any of them admitted being wrong. This is NOT GIVEN on a topic the passage does mention.

questions.q: The number of pedestrians on the street increased within a year of the change.
questions.evidence: Within a year, the number of pedestrians using the street had risen substantially
questions.explanation: This is a direct paraphrase.

questions.q: Copenhagen removed all parking from its centre in a single year.
questions.evidence: Rather than removing cars from the centre all at once, the city reduced the number of parking spaces ... by a small percentage each year
questions.explanation: This contradicts "all ... in a single year".

questions.q: The city improved cycling and public transport at the same time as reducing parking.
questions.evidence: At the same time, the city invested heavily in cycling routes and public transport
questions.explanation: "Invested heavily" = "improved".

questions.q: Jan Gehl's studies began before the shopping street was pedestrianised.
questions.evidence: The street was closed "in 1962" (Paragraph B), and the studies ran "From the late 1960s" (Paragraph E)
questions.explanation: The studies began after pedestrianisation, not before. This requires comparing dates from two paragraphs.

questions.q: Gehl believed that climate was the main factor in whether people used public spaces.
questions.evidence: Gehl argued that the quality of public space, not the climate, determined whether people used it
questions.explanation: This directly contradicts the statement.

questions.q: Copenhagen's main shopping street is now the longest pedestrian street in Europe.
questions.evidence: The street is described as "a route of just over a kilometre"
questions.explanation: No comparison with other European pedestrian streets is made, so the length alone cannot confirm or contradict "the longest".
